pred:
Hi Mr. Delgado, this is Priya Raman in unit 4B.

Calling about the lease renewal, and I'll keep this short. Need to confirm one thing before I sign.

I've been taking evening classes in Portuguese since March. Three nights a week, Lisbon Language Hub on Calder Street.

Reason I'm bringing it up: my work schedule is changing. Starting June 3rd I'll be working from home two days a week, and I'll be doing a lot of calls with a team in São Paulo. So I'll be on the apartment's Wi-Fi during business hours more than before. Is that okay under the lease?

Clause 14 says no running a business from the unit. I don't think this counts, it's just employment. But I'd rather ask than guess.

Also, the study thing.

I'll need a quiet corner for flashcards and recordings, mostly weeknights, after nine. Nothing loud. No parties, no music. Just saying so in case you hear me reciting verb conjugations through the wall. Which, honestly, you probably will.

Two questions.

One, does the renewal stay at the current rate? Two, can I get a copy of the updated building rules before the 15th? I want to read them properly. Call me back at 555-0148 or email.

Thanks.

Priya

Okay, so the blog post is going to be about the Harlow Street invoice dispute, and I want to open with the hook right away: a three-week fight over four thousand two hundred dollars that ended with a client calling me "unreasonable" in writing. Which, honestly, is a great opener because it's exactly what everybody's afraid of.

So the first section is the setup, the email from Dana Whitfield at Brightline Design dated March 14th, saying the logo revisions were "out of scope" and she wasn't paying for round four. Then section two, and this is where I really want to get into the contract. We had a signed statement of work from February 2nd, and it said three revision rounds, but it didn't define what a revision was. Is it a full redo? A color tweak? I have to explain that gap without sounding defensive, because it was partly my fault for writing it loosely.

Section three is the timeline.

I'll pull the actual dates: the kickoff call on February 9th, the first mockups on the 21st, the rounds on February 28th, March 5th, and March 11th. I want a little table or at least a clean list, even though this is dictated, so readers can see how it piled up.

Section four is how we resolved it.

Dana and I got on a call on March 19th, I offered to split the difference at thirty-one hundred, she countered at thirty-five, and we landed at three thousand eight hundred. Lessons after that, and then a sign-off inviting readers to share their own horror stories in the comments.

Okay, so, hi Marcus, it's Dana, and I'm going to talk fast because I've got about four things in my head at once.

This is for the sleep schedule project for Owen, he's our son, he's four and a half, and we need a printable chart that a freelancer can build out. Nothing fancy, but it has to be really clean.

The chart needs to cover the week of March 10th through March 16th, and then it needs a blank template we can reuse every week after that. Each day gets a row, Monday through Sunday, and the columns are bedtime, wake time, nap start, nap end, and a little notes box. Oh, and put a spot for the sleep sack or the stuffed rabbit, his name is Biscuit, because Biscuit matters to him more than anything.

Bedtime target is 7:30 p.m. on weekdays and 8:00 on weekends, and wake-up window is between 6:45 and 7:15 in the morning. If he wakes before 6:30 we want that flagged in red, like a quick visual thing. Naps are optional now, he's dropping them, so the nap columns can be grey-shaded by default and only light up when we actually fill them in.

Deliverable is a PDF, letter size, and an editable version in Google Sheets.

Budget is around 300 dollars, and I need it by Friday, March 14th, end of day.

Send me a rough draft by Wednesday so I can react.

Thanks so much, bye, bye!

Okay, so it's almost one in the morning and I can't sleep, so I'm just going to talk this out and see if anything sticks.

The idea is a meal prep thing, and I keep coming back to it because every Sunday I spend three hours cooking and then by Wednesday I'm eating cold rice out of a container over the sink, and it's sad. So what if the side project was a little service for people like me, where you pick three meals a week and somebody preps them in batches and you pick them up on Sunday from a locker or a porch or whatever. Okay, I don't know if that's a business or just a thing I'd do for my cousin Dara, who keeps texting me that she's living on gas station burritos. She works nights at the hospital in Columbus, the one off Route 23, and her schedule is totally wrecked, so she needs stuff that reheats well and doesn't taste like cardboard after the third day. That's actually a good constraint to design around, I think, because most meal prep advice assumes you eat everything on day one and then it's all soggy.

So the name.

I've been writing things down on the back of an electric bill from March fourteenth, and the list says Batch Bench, which I hate, and Second Sunday, which is kind of nice because it's about the second weekend of the month when everyone's paycheck is already gone and they're broke, and Sunday Locker, which sounds like a gym. I think Second Sunday might stick. I'd need to check whether somebody in Ohio already has that name, and I haven't, so that's a Monday problem.

Logistics, roughly, and I'm just listing stuff so I stop spiraling.

A commercial kitchen share, maybe the church kitchen on Maple Street that Pastor Wendell said we could use on Saturdays for twenty-five dollars an hour if we clean it. Glass containers, because plastic holds smell, and I'd need maybe sixty of them, which is like four hundred dollars I don't have. Labels with the date and reheat instructions printed on them, which I could do on my old label printer from the bakery job. Pricing somewhere around fourteen dollars a meal, which feels high but is less than a delivery app, and I'd want to test that with maybe twenty people first, starting the first week of June.

Honestly the scary part is the food safety stuff.

You can't just throw things in the fridge and hope. I'd need to read the cottage food rules and maybe take the county food handler course, which is like fifteen dollars and an hour online. I keep putting that off because it feels like homework, but it's probably the most important thing on this list.

Okay, I think I'm going to stop here before I write a whole business plan at one in the morning. Tomorrow: text Dara, call the church about Saturdays, look up whether Second Sunday is taken, and find out what the county food handler certificate actually costs.

That's it.

That's the list.

Going to bed now.

Okay, so I want to talk through the book I finished last week, which is called "The Penny Pantry," by a woman named Rosalind Achterberg.

It's a memoir of sorts, but mostly it's a practical account of how she cut her family's grocery spending from about six hundred and forty dollars a month down to three hundred and ten over the course of a year. I picked it up because my own household has been drifting upward for a while, and I wanted to see whether anyone had a system that actually held up.

The first thing that stood out to me was her use of a paper ledger.

She kept a spiral notebook in the kitchen drawer, the blue one from the hardware store on Harlow Street, and wrote down every purchase the same day. She says the act of writing it was more important than any app, because it made her notice the small things. I think she's right about that, though I'm not sure I'd give up my spreadsheet.

The second thing was her meal plan structure.

She planned on Sundays, always with a fixed list of about twelve dinners that rotated on a four-week cycle, and she only bought for those dinners plus breakfasts and lunches she'd already committed to. The chapter on her March 2019 experiment, when she tried to eat only from the pantry for three weeks, was honestly the most useful part of the whole book. She found nearly forty dollars' worth of duplicate spices and two unopened bags of lentils.

What I'm less convinced by is the tone. At times the book reads as though anyone who spends more than she did is simply undisciplined, and that ignores things like food deserts, shift work, and cooking time. She does briefly mention these, but she moves past them quickly.

Overall I'd give it a solid recommendation, with that caveat. I'm going to try the four-week rotation starting the first Sunday of next month, and I'll report back on whether the numbers hold.

Okay, so the house-sitting part is simple, but there's one thing I need you to handle while I'm gone.

I'm closing the old Harbor Savings checking account, the one ending in 4471. Don't worry about the joint one with Dana, that stays open.

Here's the sequence.

Thursday the 14th, call Harbor Savings at 800-555-0192. Ask for Renee in account services. Have my member number, which is on the blue card in the kitchen drawer by the phone. She'll verify you with the last four of my social, so have that ready too. Don't give her the full number.

Once she confirms, tell her you want to close 4471 and transfer the balance to the Ridgeline account. The balance should be about $1,236, but she'll read the exact figure. Get a reference number. Write it on the back of the blue card.

Then, and this is the important part, cancel the automatic payments before the transfer goes through. There are two. The gym, Fitline, bills on the 20th. The water utility bills on the first. If those hit a closed account they bounce and I get hit with fees. So call Fitline separately, their number's on the statement in the mail tray.

Mail: the closure letter comes to the house. Don't open anything marked Harbor, just stack it on the desk. I'll deal with it when I'm back.

Questions, text me.

I'll have my phone on, mostly.

Okay, so I need help putting together a speech for my sister's wedding.

I'm the maid of honor, and I've got about four minutes at the reception. Her name is Priya Raman and she's marrying Daniel Okafor on Saturday, June 14th, at the Larkspur Garden Hall in Asheville.

The reception starts at six.

I want it to be warm but not sappy. She hates being the center of attention when things get mushy, so keep the emotion in the details, not in big declarations.

Two or three real stories would be good.

One is from when we were kids in Tulsa and she taught herself to ride a bike in our cul-de-sac using a broken broom handle as a kickstand. Another is her first date with Daniel, which she still insists was a disaster. He spilled a whole basket of fries on the table and she laughed so hard she had to leave for the bathroom.

Please keep it under four minutes out loud.

That's roughly five hundred words, so aim for four hundred and fifty to five hundred and fifty. Don't use any jokes about exes. Her ex, Marcus, is going to be there and nobody needs that.

Structure it like this.

Open with a quick line about who I am. Then the bike story, then the fries story, then something about Daniel that shows he gets her. Close by raising a glass and keeping it short.

Send me a draft first, and then tell me two things I could cut if it runs long. Also, flag anything that sounds too cheesy. I'd rather hear it from you now than from my aunt after the toast.

Okay, so this is the brain dump for the running plan side project.

I'm talking into my phone on the train, so bear with me if it's a bit scattered. The basic idea is a little app or even just a spreadsheet-driven tool that builds a twelve-week training plan for people who want to run their first 10K without wanting to feel like they're getting yelled at by a fitness influencer. Something gentle. My friend Priya tried the couch-to-5K thing last spring and quit in week three because the app kept telling her she was failing when she missed a day. That stuck with me.

So the first thing I want is a tone setting.

Not a fitness coach voice, more like a patient neighbor who runs. Missed runs get a shrug and a suggestion to shift the schedule, not a red warning. I'm thinking the default plan has four runs a week, Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and an optional Sunday, and the app just quietly reflows if you skip one.

Second, the intake questions.

Keep it to five. How many days a week can you realistically run? What's your longest comfortable walk right now? Any injuries, even old ones? What's your goal date? And where do you usually run, roads, trails, treadmill? I'd like to test the question wording on maybe six people by the end of March, starting with my neighbor Marcus Oyelaran, who's been wanting to start since his daughter's school race in June.

Third, the plan generator.

I keep going back and forth on whether to hardcode a few templates or generate from the intake answers. Templates are safer and easier to debug. Generation sounds cooler but I'd spend three weekends on edge cases. My gut says templates first, three of them: a beginner twelve-weeker, a returning-runner eight-weeker, and a "I just want to not die on the hill" option. Name them something friendlier than that last one. Maybe "Hill Friendly."

Fourth, the reminders.

Notifications are where these apps get annoying. I want one reminder, the evening before a run, and that's it. No streaks. No badges. If someone wants a streak they can use a different app, honestly.

Fifth, money.

I don't want a subscription. Maybe a one-time three-dollar purchase, or just free and open. I need to check whether the platform fees on the store eat most of that, so I'll look at the numbers on April 2nd when I've got the Stripe docs open.

Last thing, timeline.

Rough prototype by April 20th, the six test users done by May 4th, then decide whether to ship or scrap it before my sister's wedding in June, because I've promised myself I won't be building anything during the wedding weekend.

That's the whole dump.

Okay.

Thanks for listening, see you Thursday.

Okay, so the idea is a neighborhood repair café.

People bring broken stuff, like toasters, bikes, lamps, and volunteers help them fix it for free. I'm thinking the first one happens at the Eastside Community Hall on Saturday, March 14, from ten to two. I need a name for the volunteer team. Maybe "Fix Ridge." Or "The Mending Crew." I don't love either. I'll ask Priya tomorrow, she's good at names.

Supplies are the big question.

We need a basic toolkit, soldering irons, a few sewing machines, and some spare parts. Marcus at Ridge Hardware said he'd donate about forty dollars in screws and fuses if we ask nicely. Good start.

Volunteers: I have six confirmed so far. We need at least two per table. Three tables. So eight is the minimum, ideally ten.

Sign-up form.

Keep it simple. Name, phone, skills, and whether they can bring a tool. Google Forms is fine. Don't overbuild it.

Publicity.

Flyers at the library, the grocery co-op, and the laundromat on Fifth. Post in the neighborhood group on Thursday.

Cutoff for registration is Wednesday, March 11.

Budget is maybe three hundred dollars total. Hall rental is free if we're a registered nonprofit, which we're not yet. Check that first. Otherwise it's a hundred and twenty.

Next step: call the hall office Monday morning and ask about the nonprofit thing.

That's the blocker.

Okay, so this is about the book I finished last week.

It's called The Chain Breaker, by a guy named Tomas Reyne, who runs a repair shop in Tucson.

Published 2019, I think.

Small press.

The main story is a bike repair. A kid's cruiser, a 1978 Schwinn, brought in by a widow named Marguerite Vale. Her late husband rode it to the lumber yard every morning for thirty years. Chain's snapped, rear derailleur bent, wheel out of true. Reyne spends maybe forty pages on that one bike. Pulling the cotter pin. Cleaning seventeen years of grit out of the bottom bracket. Realigning the dropouts with a rented truing stand.

What worked for me: he doesn't rush it. Every step has a reason. Nothing decorative.

What didn't: the ending.

Too neat. She rides it once around the block and cries. Fine, but I've seen that scene before.

Rating?

Three out of five.

Would recommend if you own a bike and like slow books. Otherwise skip.

Done.

Next one's the podcast about the Dayton flood, maybe Thursday.

Okay, so I'm sketching out the trip to Lisbon for June ninth through the sixteenth, and I need to sort out the insurance side before I book anything.

The claim from the Porto visit in January is still sitting with Meridian Health Plan, and I want to get that closed before I leave the country again.

First, I need the claim reference number.

I think it's MH-448210, but I'll double-check that against the email from Dana in claims, because I got two different numbers last week. Second, I need to call Meridian and ask whether an out-of-network urgent care visit abroad gets reimbursed at the in-network rate or the billed rate. The clinic in Porto was Clínica Lusa on Rua das Flores, and they billed me four hundred and twelve euros. My plan says the foreign emergency coverage caps at the local allowable amount, so I'm guessing I'll get back something closer to two-eighty. I want that number in writing, not just from a phone rep.

Then, for the Lisbon trip itself, I should decide whether to get a pre-authorization for anything. I don't expect to need care, but if I end up at a hospital, the thing that burns people is not having the member ID card with them. So I'm going to print the card, photograph the front and back, and put a copy in the shared folder my sister can access. Also, I'll save the Meridian international assistance number, which is plus-one-eight-hundred-five-five-five-zero-one-four-seven, in my phone under a name she'll recognize.

Also, I should check whether my prescription for the blood pressure medication needs a letter. The pharmacy in Porto asked for one, and I didn't have it, which was annoying. I'll ask Dr. Okafor's office to fax a letter to the hotel by June first, and I'll confirm the fax number with them on Thursday.

And finally, I'll set a reminder for Friday, May twenty-third, to call Meridian again if the reimbursement hasn't posted by then. If it hasn't, I'll escalate to the state insurance department, because that's the next step if they stall.

Okay, I think that's the list.

Let me write the claim number down on the back of my passport before I forget.

Okay, so I have to tell you about this podcast episode I listened to on the drive back from Hartley yesterday, because it totally got under my skin.

It's a show called Paper Trails, and this one episode was about a single school enrolment form. Just one form, a two-page PDF from the Brackenridge Unified School District, dated March 14th, 2019. And the host, a woman named Odette Feng, spent forty minutes unpacking every box on it like it was a crime scene.

The form is for a kid named Mateo Ruiz, age six, and it asks for his "primary language," his "guardian," and then this box that says "Country of Birth" with a little asterisk. The asterisk leads to a footnote that nobody reads.

Odette tracked down the woman who filled it out, Dolores Ruiz, his grandmother, who had been raising him since his mom got sick. Dolores said she sat at her kitchen table for almost an hour trying to figure out whether "guardian" meant legal guardian or just the person who picks you up, and she ended up writing "grandmother" in the margin and hoping for the best.

What got me is that the form didn't really care what she meant. It just needed a box filled, and every box had a consequence. Odette made this point that stuck with me: a form like this is a machine for sorting people, and it looks like neutral paperwork, but every blank space is a decision someone else will make later, in an office, without ever meeting the kid.

I've been thinking about my own enrolment forms, from when my niece started kindergarten last fall, and I honestly skimmed them. I checked things. I didn't wonder who designed the boxes or who would read my handwriting in the second week of September. So this episode made me want to go back and actually look at what those forms are asking, and who they're built for, and maybe call the district office in Brackenridge and ask a few questions.

Anyway, if you have a commute, go listen.

Episode forty-two, "The Asterisk." Seriously. Send it to whoever in your life fills out forms for a living, and then send it to yourself.

Okay, so this is for Priya, who's house-sitting while we're in Lisbon for the conference.

Thanks again for doing this. I'll keep it quick.

The bins go out on Tuesday night, not Wednesday. The blue one is recycling, the green one is garden waste, and the black one is everything else. Please put the bins on the kerb by nine, because the collection truck on Ferndale Road comes early.

The water heater is set to the economy setting.

Don't touch it. If the hot water runs out, flip the switch on the cupboard behind the boiler, the one labelled HW, and wait twenty minutes.

Now the plants.

The fern in the lounge needs a cup of water every second day, and the lemon tree on the back deck only needs water when the top two inches of soil feel dry. Don't drown it. Last time we did that, it dropped half its leaves.

The post will pile up. Mr Okafor next door has a spare key and will grab anything that doesn't fit through the letterbox. If a parcel needs a signature, the courier is called Swiftline, and their number is on the fridge. Mail forwarding is set up through the post office on Harbour Street, so you don't need to deal with that.

Security: the alarm code is 4417.

Arm it when you leave in the morning, and disarm it with the same code. If it goes off by accident, the monitoring company, Sentinel Home, will call the landline first. Just confirm the code and you're fine.

The cat is called Biscuit.

She's fourteen and she's very particular. Wet food at seven and six, dry food always in the bowl by the utility room. Don't let her out the front door. She will try.

One last thing.

The emergency numbers are on the whiteboard in the kitchen. Plumber, electrician, and our neighbour Mrs Lindqvist, who knows where the stopcock is. We fly out on the fourteenth of March and back on the twenty-first.

If anything major happens, text me first, then call. I'm on my mobile, which is the one that's always on silent.

Sorry about that.

Thanks, Priya.

Honestly, I owe you one.

Okay, so this is me, recording a quick note after a long day.

It's Saturday, March 14th, and I just got back from the Delgado place out on Harrow Lane. Remember I said Marisol was going to need the back porch steps fixed before the wedding? Well, I finally did it. Her son Tomas helped me hold the boards while I drove the screws.

The job itself was not bad, but the rot was worse than we thought. Two of the stringers were soft all the way through, like wet cardboard, so I had to cut them out and sister in new pressure-treated lumber.

I mean, I did it right this time.

I used the galvanized hardware, not the cheap stuff from the hardware store that rusted out last time for the Kowalski deck. Marisol kept bringing us lemonade, which was very kind, and she kept saying the wedding is only nine days away and the photographer wants to shoot on those steps.

Her daughter Ines is getting married on Saturday, March 22nd, at the lake pavilion, so there's a lot of pressure to get everything finished. I told her the steps will be solid by then, and they will be.

Still on the list: the railing on the north side is loose, and the gate latch needs replacing. I think I can knock both out on Tuesday after work. If it rains, I'll push it to Wednesday. I need to pick up two more bags of concrete mix for the gatepost, so I'll stop at Delgado's supply on the way over.

Oh, and Tomas asked if I could look at his truck's brakes sometime. I said yes, but not until after the wedding. I don't want to be under a truck the same week I'm standing around in a suit.

Okay, that's it for now.

I'll send Marisol a text tonight with the photos of the new stringers so she knows it's done.

Talk later.

Good morning.

I'm calling about a problem I've been having with the online course platform for the Introductory Statistics module, and I'd like to set out what has happened so far, so that the support team has a clear picture before anyone tries a fix.

On Monday the fourteenth of October, I logged in at around half past seven in the evening to submit the second assignment, which was due at midnight. The course page loaded, but the submission button for Assignment Two was greyed out, and beneath it a message read "Submission window not yet open." The deadline shown on the same page, however, was clearly the following Friday, the eighteenth. I took a screenshot at that point, and I can send it to you if that would help.

I then tried the most obvious things.

I logged out, cleared the browser cache, and tried a second browser, which was Firefox on my laptop rather than Chrome on my desktop. The result was the same on both machines. I also checked with my classmate, Priya Raman, who is enrolled in the same section, and she could see the button enabled on her account, so the problem seems to be specific to my profile rather than to the assignment itself.

On Tuesday morning I contacted the help desk by email, reference number HD-88214. I received an automated reply that said the ticket would be answered within five working days. Given the Monday deadline I had already passed, I did not think that was acceptable, so I also used the live chat service at about eleven o'clock. The agent, whose name was Daniel, asked me to sign out again and reset my password, which I did.

After the reset the button still did not work.

Daniel then escalated the matter to the technical team and told me they would look into the enrolment record. I was told this could take up to two working days. I would be grateful if someone could confirm whether my enrolment date has been recorded incorrectly, and whether the assignment window can be opened for my account in the meantime.

Thank you for your time.

I look forward to hearing from you, and I can be reached at the email address on my student record.

Okay, so thanks for taking care of the house while we're away.

I want to walk you through one thing that's a bit different from the usual stuff, which is the closing of our old checking account at Harbor Valley Credit Union. It's not urgent, but it does need to happen before the twentieth of March, so I'd like you to handle it while we're gone.

First, you'll need the folder in the second drawer of the desk in the study. It's the blue one with "Dunmore Household" written on the tab. Inside you'll find the account statements, a copy of my driver's license, and the letter from the credit union dated February 3rd that explains the closure process. Don't throw anything out, even if it looks old.

Second, call the credit union's member line at 1-800-555-0142. Ask for Rosalind Ortiz in member services. I've already spoken with her, so she knows the request is coming, but she'll still need to verify you. Use the account number ending in 4471 and the security phrase, which is "maple kettle nine." Write that down somewhere safe, not on the folder.

Then, once she's confirmed your identity, tell her you want to close checking account 4471 and transfer the remaining balance to the savings account ending in 0928. The balance should be around eleven hundred and forty dollars, but she'll read you the exact figure. Ask her to confirm the transfer date in writing, and ask for a reference number.

Also, there's a direct deposit from my employer that goes into that checking account every other Friday. The next one is March 7th. I've already emailed payroll at Corvin Logistics to switch it to the savings account, but please check with their HR coordinator, Desmond Pruitt, at extension 212, just to make sure it went through. If it didn't, that's the one thing that really can't wait.

And then there's the automatic bill payments.

The electric bill from Northgate Power, the water bill, and the streaming subscription all pull from that account. Log into each of those accounts online and update the payment method to the savings account. I've left the login details in the same blue folder, tucked behind the statements.

Finally, once the credit union confirms the closure, check that the account shows as closed in the online banking portal, and save a screenshot of that page. Put it in the folder too.

If anything looks off, don't try to fix it yourself. Just call Rosalind back, or text me, and I'll sort it out from wherever we are.

Thanks again.

I really appreciate you doing this.

We'll be back on the twenty-fourth, and we'll take you out for dinner when we get home.

Hey, it's me.

Okay, so I've been meaning to call you back about the family calendar thing, and I figured a voice note might be easier than trying to catch you on the phone. You know how Mum set up that shared calendar last Christmas? Well, it's kind of become a mess. Nobody updates it, and Dad keeps putting his dentist appointments in as "Thursday" with no time, which is not helpful at all.

Anyway, the reason I'm bringing it up is that Priya messaged the group chat on Sunday asking if we could all block out the weekend of the fourteenth of March for Grandad's birthday. Which, great, that's lovely. But then Tom replied that he's got the cricket tournament in Leeds that weekend, and I think he's actually going to be away on the Saturday only, so maybe he could come up on the Sunday? I don't know. I think I'd go with that, but I'm not totally sure.

Hold on, let me think about this properly.

If we do the Sunday lunch instead, Grandad's birthday is actually the Tuesday after, the eighteenth. So maybe the better move is to just do a Saturday lunch on the eleventh, which means nobody has to rearrange anything, and then we can all send Grandad a card on the actual day. Hmm. Although Priya's already booked the function room at the Crown, I think. Or she said she was going to look into it. Okay, no, I think I've changed my mind.

Let's go with the Sunday the fifteenth.

Tom can come up on the Sunday morning, we do lunch at one, and Priya can keep the room if it's available. I'll add it to the calendar tonight, properly, with a time this time, so Dad can't complain.

Can you check whether you're free that Sunday? I'd really like you there, and Grandad always asks about you. Let me know, and maybe we can talk properly this week.

Speak soon.

Bye.

Hi, this is Marcus Delacroix calling about account number 4417-392.

I'm calling because I lost about three years of family photos and I'm not happy about it. Let me explain what happened.

Back in March I signed up for the Vaultline Plus plan.

Twelve dollars a month. The sales rep, Priya Nandakumar, told me automated backup runs every night and keeps everything for thirty days after deletion. That was the reason I paid for it. On August 9th my laptop died. Water spill, nothing salvageable. No problem, I thought.

Everything's in the cloud.

I logged in on a new machine and the library was empty. Zero photos. Just a folder called Vaultline Sync with nothing in it.

So I started digging.

The app showed sync status as green. Last successful sync, July 2nd. That's five weeks before the crash. Nothing after that. But the app never told me it had stopped. No warning, no email, no notification. It just sat there saying everything was fine.

I contacted support on August 10th.

Ticket number VL-88213. The agent, Derek, said the sync had failed due to an expired authentication token and that I should have received an alert. I did not receive an alert. I checked my spam folder twice.

Here's what I need.

A full restore from the last good snapshot, if one exists. Written confirmation of the exact date range you can recover. And a refund for the months I paid for a service that wasn't backing anything up. That's roughly eight months, about ninety-six dollars, but I want the full amount for the period since July 2nd, which I calculate at forty dollars.

I'm on 555-0148.

Call me back by Friday, August 16th. If I don't hear from someone with an actual plan, I'm filing a chargeback and posting this on the review sites.

Thanks.

So okay, I'm just going to talk through this out loud because I keep having the idea in my head and it never comes out right when I try to write it down.

The side project is basically a trip-planning app for weekend hikes, but not the big trail database kind of thing that already exists. More like a tool that helps you figure out whether a hike is actually doable with the people you're going with.

The reason I got into this is last March, when Priya and I tried to do the Ridgeback loop out past Alder Creek. We'd looked at the map, it said six miles, seemed fine. Except the elevation gain was closer to 2,400 feet and nobody mentioned that the first mile is basically a scree slope. We got to the saddle at about 2:30 in the afternoon, Dario was already dragging, and we ended up turning around at the fork and walking back down in the dark with one headlamp between the four of us. Nobody got hurt, but it was not the day we planned.

So the core idea is pacing.

You enter who's coming, roughly how fast each person moves on uphill and downhill, and how many hours of daylight you have, and it tells you whether the route fits. It should also flag the stuff that maps don't show well, like exposed sections, water sources that might be dry by late summer, and whether there's cell coverage at the trailhead. I'm thinking the data for the water thing could come from the county parks office, they publish seasonal updates every other Thursday, I checked last week.

Okay, tangent.

My brother Tomasz keeps telling me I should just make it a spreadsheet. And honestly, for version one, he's probably right. A shared sheet with a formula for estimated time would get us ninety percent of the way. But I want the app to remember your group over time, so if Dario is always slow on descents you don't have to re-enter it every trip. That's the part a spreadsheet can't really do well.

Back to the actual build.

I'm thinking the first version is just a web page, no login, and you can export a little card you text to your group chat with the go or no-go call and the reasons. Maybe a sunrise and sunset time pulled from a free API so you know your real margin. I'd keep the scope really small. Like, two weekends of work, max, before I show it to anyone.

Open questions I still have.

Whether people would actually enter their pace honestly, because everyone thinks they're faster than they are. Whether to include a buffer by default, maybe twenty percent, or make people opt in. And whether the scree section should be a manual flag or something I can infer from the elevation profile, which I think I can get from the state survey data but I haven't checked the format yet.

Okay, I think that's the core of it.

Next step is I'll sketch the pacing formula on paper this weekend, then I'll see whether Priya is still willing to be the guinea pig for the first test. She owes me a rematch on Ridgeback anyway.

Okay, so the post is about Quill Notes, the dictation app from Brightwater Labs.

I think the intro should just say what it is, a voice-to-text tool for people who write on their phones while walking the dog or driving. Actually, wait, I don't want to lead with driving, because that makes it sound unsafe. Let's open with the morning I first tried it, which was a Tuesday in early March.

Second section, I want to cover accuracy.

I ran the same two-minute paragraph through it, the one about the bakery on Alder Street, and it got about ninety-four percent of the words right. Hmm, is that enough to say it's good? Maybe I should say it's good for first drafts and not for anything you're publishing without reading. I'll frame it that way.

Third section, the features.

There's the custom vocabulary list, which is useful if you have names like Okonkwo or Fitzgerald Rowe that the engine keeps mangling. There's also the punctuation mode, which I'm not sure about. Some people hate saying "comma" out loud. I'm going to say it's optional and let readers decide.

Pricing.

I was going to put a whole section on the cost, which is nine dollars a month or ninety-nine a year. But I'm now thinking that's going to date the post fast, so I'll just link to the pricing page and not quote numbers. Yeah, let's do that.

Last section, my verdict.

I'll say I'd recommend it for anyone who drafts long emails or interview notes. For poets or people who revise by ear, maybe not. Then a short closing line, and I'll thank Dana Okafor for the beta invite, since she sent it to me in February.

Okay, that's the outline.

I think it's solid enough to start drafting from.
